name: Tessellate Distribution
description:
Tessellate Distribution is not a label but presents itself as one — a fiction maintained for legal plausibility. In practice, it is a decentralized encrypted mesh network for music distribution, operating across all tiers of GLMZ through a cell structure in which no single node knows the full map. Founded around 2215 by a loose coalition of music archivists, BCI privacy advocates, and former Vantablack employees who left under various circumstances ranging from principled resignation to termination with prejudice, Tessellate exists to move music that the licensed distribution infrastructure will not carry: politically banned content, unlicensed neural-feed recordings, live bootlegs, AI-generated music released without corporate authorization, and work by artists under Vantablack non-compete orders.

The network's operational model resembles a dead-drop system adapted for digital media. Artists submit encrypted packages to any of several dozen known entry nodes — physical drop points in Circuit markets, Shelf community spaces, and certain Tier 3 cafes and bookshops. The packages propagate through the mesh according to an algorithm that distributes routing decisions across multiple nodes, making any single point insufficient to reconstruct the network's topology. Listeners access Tessellate content through a lightweight BCI application that looks, on a compliance scan, like a standard meditation feed. The content itself is watermarked with an interlocking tile pattern — the network's name — which serves as both branding and authenticity verification.
creator: Founding coalition (attributed to 'the Archivists,' no public identities confirmed)
genre: All genres — distribution network, not genre-specific
audience: Artists and listeners across all tiers who need distribution outside Vantablack's compliance framework; BCI privacy advocates; underground music communities; archivists
cultural_impact: Tessellate has become the primary distribution infrastructure for banned and restricted music in GLMZ, and its cross-tier reach makes it unusual among underground networks, which typically serve only the Shelf and lower Circuit. The network's presence in Tier 3 and even occasional Tier 4 spaces has created unexpected cultural cross-pollination — Spire-adjacent listeners encountering raw Shelf protest music, Shelf artists discovering that their work has found audiences they never imagined reaching. For Vantablack's compliance division, Tessellate represents a persistent and genuinely difficult problem: unlike pirate radio, it has no physical signal to triangulate, and unlike physical media trading, it leaves no obvious object to seize.
known_fans: Underground club promoters who use it to source sets
story_hooks: A Tessellate entry node — a Circuit bookshop whose owner has quietly been running drops for two years — has been raided by a Vantablack compliance team accompanied by city enforcement. The owner is in custody. The node's physical drives were seized but the mesh encryption held. Someone needs to determine whether the raid was targeted intelligence or random enforcement, because if it was targeted, other nodes are at risk.

An artist has submitted a package to Tessellate containing recordings that, according to a source, include illegally obtained BCI audio — recordings made directly from someone's neural feed without consent. The archivists are divided: the content is politically explosive and genuinely important, but distributing it may implicate the network in a serious crime and expose the source to danger.

A Tessellate node deep in the Tier 4 corporate district has gone silent — no packages in or out for ten days. The node's operator was a Vantablack employee who had been leaking compliance-cleared master recordings of artists under non-compete orders. Someone needs to find out if the operator is compromised, dead, or simply scared, and whether the node's location has been burned.
